IDA treatment is a favorite boards topic because the answer isn't just give iron — you must treat the underlying cause first, or you'll miss a GI malignancy while chasing a lab value. First-line therapy is oral iron: ferrous sulfate, gluconate, or fumarate, taken on an empty stomach to maximize absorption, doses spaced six hours apart, roughly 200 milligrams of elemental iron daily, continued for more than six months so you replete stores, not just normalize hemoglobin. Absorption enhancers worth knowing: citric acid, vitamin C, and fructose. Inhibitors, a classic exam distractor: tea polyphenols, phytates in bran, calcium-phosphate complexes, tannins, and soy protein — so counsel patients to separate iron from tea, dairy, or antacids. Parenteral iron is reserved for hypersensitivity or anaphylactoid reactions to oral iron, or when you need to replenish body iron rapidly and oral therapy has failed. Memorize the expected response timeline, since boards love to test it: reticulocytosis peaks at 7 to 10 days, the hemoglobin deficit is halved by 1 month, and hemoglobin normalizes by 6 to 8 weeks. If that timeline isn't met, think through the differential for oral iron failure: continued hemorrhage, poor compliance, concurrent ascorbic acid deficiency, wrong diagnosis altogether, mixed anemia, malabsorption, or hepcidin elevation from inflammation or a TMPRSS6 mutation causing IRIDA.

keypoints: Treat the underlying cause first — don't just replace iron blindly
Oral iron: ferrous salts, empty stomach, ~200mg/day, continue >6 months
Enhance with vitamin C; avoid tea, phytates, calcium at same time
Expected response: retic peak 7-10d, Hb deficit halved at 1mo, normal by 6-8wk
Failure causes: ongoing bleed, poor compliance, wrong diagnosis, IRIDA
segments.voiceover: Always treat the underlying cause, not just the iron level. First-line is oral ferrous iron on an empty stomach, about 200 milligrams daily, continued past six months to fully replete stores. Vitamin C boosts absorption; tea, phytates, and calcium block it. Expect reticulocytosis by 7 to 10 days, hemoglobin deficit halved by 1 month, and normal hemoglobin by 6 to 8 weeks. If that response doesn't happen, think ongoing bleeding, poor compliance, wrong diagnosis, or hepcidin-driven IRIDA.

This diagram shows hemoglobin synthesis as two coordinated processes inside the erythroblast: iron delivery and heme biosynthesis. On the right, the transferrin cycle: transferrin receptor binds iron-loaded transferrin, it's endocytosed, iron drops into the cytoplasmic iron pool, and apo-transferrin recycles out. That iron pool does double duty, it feeds mitochondrial heme synthesis, and it stabilizes iron-sulfur clusters on IRE binding protein, which controls translation of ALAS-2, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis. High iron favors ALAS-2 and globin mRNA translation together, keeping heme and globin production matched. The heme pathway itself, glycine plus B6 plus succinyl-CoA form delta-ALA, then porphobilinogen, then porphyrinogen intermediates, finishing in mitochondria where protoporphyrin plus ferrous iron makes heme. Four hemes combine with two alpha and two beta globin chains to form hemoglobin. High-yield point, ALAS-2 is iron- and erythropoietin-regulated and rate-limiting, defects anywhere in this pathway cause sideroblastic anemias or porphyrias, the topics of the next slides.

keypoints: ALAS-2 = rate-limiting, iron-regulated enzyme of heme synthesis
IRE-BP/Fe-S senses iron -> controls ALAS-2 mRNA translation
Heme + globin synthesis are iron-coordinated
Pathway defects -> sideroblastic anemia or porphyria
segments.voiceover: The key takeaway, ALAS-2 is the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis, and it's controlled by iron availability through the IRE binding protein and iron-sulfur cluster system. This keeps heme production matched to both iron supply and globin chain synthesis. Remember that enzyme defects anywhere along this heme biosynthetic pathway lead to either sideroblastic anemia, when early steps in mitochondria are affected, or a porphyria, when later steps are affected.

This slide classifies sideroblastic anemias, defined by pathologic iron deposits in erythroblast mitochondria, into hereditary and acquired forms. The classic hereditary cause is X-linked sideroblastic anemia, XLSA, from ALAS2 mutations, the same rate-limiting heme synthesis enzyme from the last slide, and the single most testable hereditary cause. Other hereditary causes include SLC25A38 and glutaredoxin 5 deficiency. Recognize these syndromic names, XLSA with ataxia from ABCB7 mutations disrupting iron-sulfur cluster maturation, MLASA, myopathy, lactic acidosis, sideroblastic anemia, SIFD, sideroblastic anemia with B-cell immunodeficiency, and Pearson syndrome, a mitochondrial cytopathy from large mitochondrial DNA deletions. On the acquired side, the major clonal cause is MDS with ring sideroblasts. But the high-yield exam favorite is reversible sideroblastic anemia, caused by alcoholism, lead poisoning, drugs like isoniazid, chloramphenicol, linezolid, and cyclosporine, copper deficiency, or hypothermia. These matter clinically because removing the cause, stopping the drug, adding pyridoxine for isoniazid, correcting copper, reverses the anemia.

keypoints: XLSA (ALAS2 mutation) = most common hereditary SA
ABCB7 -> XLSA/ataxia; mtDNA deletion -> Pearson syndrome
MDS-RS = major acquired clonal cause
Reversible: alcohol, lead, isoniazid/chloramphenicol/linezolid, copper deficiency, hypothermia
Isoniazid toxicity treated with B6 (pyridoxine)
segments.voiceover: Know XLSA from ALAS2 mutation as the classic hereditary sideroblastic anemia, and MDS with ring sideroblasts as the major acquired clonal cause. For exams, focus on reversible causes, alcohol, lead poisoning, drugs including isoniazid, chloramphenicol, linezolid, and cyclosporine, copper deficiency, and hypothermia. Isoniazid causes sideroblastic anemia through B6 antagonism, so it's treated with pyridoxine supplementation.

This slide shows the morphologic hallmarks of sideroblastic anemia. On electron microscopy, iron-laden mitochondria cluster around the nucleus. On Prussian blue stain, this appears as a ring sideroblast, iron granules encircling at least one-third of the nuclear circumference, the diagnostic finding for sideroblastic anemia and MDS with ring sideroblasts. On peripheral smear, severe disease shows a dimorphic red cell population, one normal and one hypochromic microcytic; mild disease shows uniform hypochromic microcytic cells that can mimic iron deficiency anemia. You may also see siderocytes, mature red cells retaining iron granules, and Pappenheimer bodies, irregular basophilic iron inclusions on Wright stain, distinct from the single round Howell-Jolly bodies of nuclear remnants. The unifying lab pattern is excess total body iron, elevated serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation, the opposite of iron deficiency anemia, and the key discriminator on boards.

keypoints: Ring sideroblast = iron in >=1/3 of nuclear circumference (Prussian blue)
Diagnostic for sideroblastic anemia and MDS-RS
Mild SA can mimic iron deficiency (hypochromic microcytic)
SA labs: ↑ serum iron, ↑ ferritin, ↑ transferrin sat (opposite of IDA)
Pappenheimer bodies (iron, irregular) vs Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear, round)
segments.voiceover: The must-know finding is the ring sideroblast, iron granules encircling at least one-third of the nucleus on Prussian blue stain, diagnostic for sideroblastic anemia and MDS with ring sideroblasts. Mild disease looks hypochromic and microcytic, so it can be confused with iron deficiency, but the labs are opposite, with elevated serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation. Also distinguish Pappenheimer bodies, irregular iron inclusions, from Howell-Jolly bodies, which are round nuclear remnants.

This diagram maps each heme biosynthesis enzyme to its corresponding porphyria when deficient, a classic boards exercise. The pathway starts in mitochondria, glycine plus succinyl-CoA form ALA via ALA synthase, feedback-inhibited by hemin. In the cytosol, ALA dehydratase deficiency causes ALA dehydratase porphyria, very rare. Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, AIP, the most important to know, autosomal dominant, roughly one to two per twenty-thousand, causing neurovisceral attacks and psychiatric symptoms, but no photosensitivity, since the accumulating ALA and PBG aren't photoactive. Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, the most common porphyria overall, about one in ten-thousand, presenting with photosensitivity, not neurovisceral disease. Further down, coproporphyrinogen oxidase and protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiencies cause hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria, both mixed neurovisceral and cutaneous. Finally, ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria. Notice lead poisoning inhibits both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which is why lead poisoning can mimic parts of this pathway.

keypoints: ALA synthase = rate-limiting, feedback-inhibited by hemin
PBG deaminase deficiency -> AIP (dominant, neurovisceral + psychiatric, no photosensitivity)
UROD deficiency -> PCT (most common porphyria, photosensitive)
Ferrochelatase deficiency -> EPP; lead inhibits ALA dehydratase & ferrochelatase
segments.voiceover: For boards, know two porphyrias cold. Acute intermittent porphyria, from porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency, is dominant and causes neurovisceral attacks with psychiatric symptoms but no photosensitivity. Porphyria cutanea tarda, from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, is the most common porphyria and causes photosensitivity without neurovisceral disease. Also remember lead poisoning inhibits both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, mimicking this pathway.

This table is the master reference for porphyrias, memorize the pattern, not every cell. Two big categories: neurovisceral porphyrias, from earlier cytosolic enzyme defects like ALA dehydratase porphyria and acute intermittent porphyria, where ALA and porphobilinogen accumulate; and photosensitive porphyrias, from later defects like congenital erythropoietic porphyria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and erythropoietic protoporphyria, where photoactive porphyrins deposit in skin. The middle enzymes, coproporphyrinogen oxidase and protoporphyrinogen oxidase, cause hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria, with mixed neurovisceral-plus-photosensitive disease. Most porphyrias are autosomal dominant, except ALA dehydratase porphyria and congenital erythropoietic porphyria, which are recessive, and erythropoietic protoporphyria, which is pseudodominant. Tissue source matters, liver porphyrias like AIP and PCT excrete precursors in urine; erythropoietic ones, CEP and EPP, arise in bone marrow, and EPP uniquely excretes protoporphyrin in feces, since it's not water soluble. The two boards-favorite porphyrias are AIP, the classic acute neurovisceral one, and PCT, the most common and classic cutaneous one.

keypoints: Early enzyme defects (ALA, PBG) -> neurovisceral (AIP, ADP)
Late enzyme defects -> photosensitive (CEP, PCT, EPP)
Middle defects (HCP, VP) -> mixed picture
Most AD except ADP & CEP (AR); EPP = pseudodominant
Liver source -> urine excretion; marrow source (EPP) -> feces
segments.voiceover: Organize the porphyrias by where the enzyme defect sits in the pathway. Early cytosolic defects, ALA dehydratase porphyria and AIP, cause neurovisceral disease from ALA and PBG accumulation. Late defects, CEP, PCT, and EPP, cause photosensitivity from porphyrin deposition in skin. Middle defects, hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria, cause a mixed picture. Most are autosomal dominant; know AIP as neurovisceral and PCT as the most common, cutaneous porphyria.

This slide focuses on porphyria cutanea tarda, the porphyria you'll see most clinically. It's the most common porphyric disorder, about one in ten-thousand, from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, either inherited or, more often, acquired. Classic precipitating factors: sun exposure, alcohol, estrogen, excessive iron intake, and infections, especially hepatitis C, strongly associated with PCT. Patients develop a photosensitive bullous dermatosis on sun-exposed skin from circulating uroporphyrins causing photoactivated tissue damage, as seen in the blistering on the hand. Unlike AIP, PCT causes no neurovisceral attacks. Treatment starts with avoiding precipitating factors, sun protection, stopping alcohol and estrogen, treating hepatitis C. First-line treatment is repeated phlebotomy, which lowers hepatic iron stores, since iron promotes the oxidative damage that inhibits UROD. Low-dose hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine is an alternative, mobilizing and helping excrete hepatic porphyrins. Phlebotomy is the boards answer for PCT treatment.

keypoints: PCT = most common porphyria (1/10,000), UROD deficiency
Triggers: sun, alcohol, estrogen, iron, hepatitis C
Presentation: photosensitive bullous dermatosis, NO neurovisceral symptoms
Treatment: phlebotomy (first line); hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine (alternative)
segments.voiceover: Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria, from UROD deficiency, triggered by sun, alcohol, estrogen, iron overload, and hepatitis C. It causes photosensitive bullous skin disease without neurovisceral symptoms, unlike AIP. First-line treatment is repeated phlebotomy to reduce hepatic iron; low-dose hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine is the alternative.

Let's cover acute intermittent porphyria, a classic boards topic. It's caused by porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency, autosomal dominant, affecting about one in twenty thousand people. Attacks are triggered by anything that induces ALA synthase — think women around their menstrual cycle, certain drugs, fasting, or stress. Clinically, abdominal pain dominates, present in about eighty five percent of attacks, along with vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, muscle weakness, and mental status changes, so it's easily mistaken for a surgical abdomen or a psychiatric illness. The classic lab clue is an elevated urine PBG to ALA ratio, roughly three to one, plus leukocytosis, hyponatremia from SIADH, and volume depletion that raises the BUN. Treatment centers on IV hemin, three to five milligrams per kilogram daily for four to five days, which suppresses ALA synthase. Also remove the precipitating factor, restore fluids and electrolytes, give high dose glucose around three hundred to five hundred grams a day as ten percent dextrose, and control pain with analgesics and narcotics.

keypoints: PBG deaminase deficiency, 1 in 20,000
Abdominal pain 85%, vomiting, tachycardia, mental change
Urine PBG:ALA ~3:1, hyponatremia, ↑BUN
Tx: IV hemin 3-5 mg/kg x 4-5d + glucose + remove trigger
segments.voiceover: For boards, remember AIP as PBG deaminase deficiency causing attacks triggered by drugs, fasting, or the menstrual cycle. Abdominal pain hits eighty five percent of patients, alongside vomiting, tachycardia, and mental status change. The lab hallmark is an elevated urine PBG to ALA ratio near three to one, with hyponatremia and a rising BUN from volume loss. Treatment is IV hemin for four to five days plus high dose glucose and removing the trigger.

Now we're moving into the hemolytic anemia section. Hemolytic anemia occurs when red blood cells are destroyed faster than they can be produced. We classify these by mechanism. Immune-mediated hemolytic anemias involve antibodies or complement attacking the RBCs. Non-immune mediated hemolytic anemias result from abnormalities of the RBC membrane, enzyme deficiencies, or acquired conditions like paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Understanding these distinctions is essential for diagnosis and treatment.

This slide maps hemoglobin destruction, comparing extravascular and intravascular hemolysis — high yield for boards. In extravascular hemolysis, splenic macrophages phagocytose red cells, breaking heme into iron, protoporphyrin, and unconjugated bilirubin, which is conjugated in the liver and excreted as urobilinogen. In intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobin is released directly into plasma, first bound by haptoglobin — which is why haptoglobin falls with intravascular hemolysis. Once haptoglobin is saturated, free hemoglobin is filtered by the kidney, reabsorbed as hemosiderin, or excreted as hemoglobinuria, while excess heme binds hemopexin and albumin as methemalbumin. Across both mechanisms, shared findings of hemolysis include anemia, elevated reticulocytes from marrow compensation, elevated LDH, and elevated indirect bilirubin. The distinguishing feature of intravascular hemolysis is hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria, while spherocytes on the smear point toward extravascular, often immune-mediated destruction.

keypoints: Extravascular: splenic macrophages → unconj. bilirubin, urobilinogen
Intravascular: free Hb binds haptoglobin (↓Hp) → filtered by kidney
Shared: ↓Hb, ↑retics, ↑LDH, ↑indirect bilirubin
Intravascular only: hemoglobinemia/hemoglobinuria
Spherocytes → extravascular/immune hemolysis
segments.voiceover: Know the shared markers of hemolysis — anemia, elevated reticulocytes, elevated LDH, and elevated indirect bilirubin. What separates the two mechanisms is intravascular hemolysis causing hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and a drop in haptoglobin, since haptoglobin gets consumed clearing free hemoglobin. Extravascular hemolysis instead shows spherocytes on smear, from splenic macrophages nibbling away red cell membrane.

This slide organizes hemolysis causes by where destruction happens, a great framework for boards. Intravascular hemolysis causes include mechanical fragmentation — think MAHA and prosthetic valves — hemolytic transfusion reactions, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, infections like malaria and clostridial sepsis, chemical or toxin exposures such as arsine gas or venom, thermal injury, and G6PD deficiency, which classically causes intravascular hemolysis during oxidative stress. Extravascular hemolysis causes cluster into membrane defects like hereditary spherocytosis and elliptocytosis, metabolic defects like pyruvate kinase deficiency, environmental causes such as infection, drug-induced or immune-mediated hemolysis, and HUS, plus abnormal or unstable hemoglobins. The photos at the bottom show the classic bedside clues to intravascular hemolysis — hemoglobinuria produces dark tea colored urine, hemoglobinemia turns the plasma pink to red, and hemosiderin deposits appear as blue granules in sloughed renal tubular epithelial cells on urinalysis, a sign of chronic intravascular hemolysis like PNH.

keypoints: Intravascular: MAHA, transfusion reaction, PNH, PCH, malaria, G6PD
Extravascular: HS/HE, PK deficiency, AIHA, HUS, hemoglobinopathies
Hemoglobinuria = dark, tea-colored urine
Hemosiderinuria (blue granules) = chronic intravascular hemolysis, e.g. PNH
segments.voiceover: Sort hemolysis causes by site. Intravascular includes mechanical fragmentation, transfusion reactions, PNH, PCH, malaria, and G6PD deficiency. Extravascular includes membrane defects like hereditary spherocytosis, metabolic defects like PK deficiency, and immune-mediated causes. Remember the bedside clues — hemoglobinuria and hemoglobinemia signal intravascular hemolysis, and hemosiderin granules in urine sediment indicate chronic intravascular hemolysis, classically seen in PNH.

This slide is a high yield classification of immune mediated hemolytic anemia by antibody thermal activity. Cold-active antibodies, active around zero to five degrees Celsius, cause cold agglutinin disease, which can be primary or secondary to lymphoproliferative disorders like Waldenstrom's, CLL, or infections — classically Mycoplasma pneumonia and infectious mononucleosis. Also in this category is paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, caused by the Donath-Landsteiner biphasic hemolysin, historically linked to syphilis and now more often to viral infections in children. Warm-active antibodies, active at body temperature, cause warm AIHA, which is idiopathic in about half of cases or secondary to lymphoproliferative disease, autoimmune disorders like lupus, viral infections, or immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy — a modern and increasingly tested association. Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia has several mechanisms worth memorizing: the drug absorption type with penicillin, neoantigen formation with quinidine, true autoimmune induction with alpha-methyldopa, and non-immune protein adsorption with first generation cephalosporins. Finally, transplant-associated hemolytic anemia occurs with ABO-mismatched stem cell or solid organ transplants, including the passenger lymphocyte syndrome.

keypoints: Cold Ab (0-5°C): CAD (Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner)
Warm Ab (37°C): idiopathic/secondary AIHA (SLE, lymphoma, checkpoint inhibitors)
Drug-induced: penicillin (absorption), quinidine (neoantigen), methyldopa (autoimmune), cephalosporins (non-immune)
Transplant-associated HA: ABO mismatch, passenger lymphocyte syndrome
segments.voiceover: Split immune hemolytic anemia by antibody temperature. Cold agglutinin disease and paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria are classically linked to Mycoplasma, mononucleosis, and the Donath-Landsteiner antibody. Warm AIHA is idiopathic or secondary to lupus, lymphoma, or checkpoint inhibitors. For drug-induced hemolysis, memorize the four mechanisms — penicillin absorption, quinidine neoantigen, methyldopa true autoimmune, and cephalosporin non-immune adsorption.

Warm AIHA is IgG mediated and this diagram shows exactly how it destroys red cells. IgG antibodies coat the red cell surface at body temperature. Macrophages in the spleen recognize the Fc portion of IgG through Fc receptors and either engulf the entire cell — complete phagocytosis — or bite off just a piece of membrane, creating a microspherocyte that circulates with reduced surface area and increased osmotic fragility. This Fc-receptor mediated phagocytosis in the spleen is the dominant mechanism, and it's why splenectomy is a treatment option for refractory warm AIHA. IgG can also fix complement, though less efficiently than IgM, activating C1 through C4 and C3, generating C3b-coated red cells that are cleared by Kupffer cells in the liver via extravascular hemolysis. So for boards, the key takeaway is warm AIHA equals IgG, extravascular hemolysis, primarily in the spleen through Fc-receptor phagocytosis, producing spherocytes on peripheral smear, and a positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG, with or without complement.

keypoints: Warm AIHA: IgG-coated RBCs at 37°C
Fc-receptor mediated phagocytosis by splenic macrophages
Partial phagocytosis → microspherocytes on smear
Extravascular hemolysis (spleen > liver); DAT+ for IgG ± C3
segments.voiceover: Warm AIHA is driven by IgG coating red cells at body temperature. Splenic macrophages use Fc receptors to phagocytose these cells, either whole or in part, and partial bites create microspherocytes, the classic smear finding. This is extravascular hemolysis, mainly in the spleen, and the direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG, sometimes with complement too.

Cold AIHA works completely differently — it's IgM and complement mediated. IgM antibodies have increased activity around zero degrees Celsius and decreased activity near thirty seven, so they bind C1q and red cells in the cooler peripheral circulation, like the fingertips, nose, and ears. As blood returns to the warmer central circulation, IgM dissociates, but it has already activated the classical complement pathway through C4, C2, and C3, depositing C3b on the red cell surface. C3b-opsonized cells are cleared extravascularly by Kupffer cells in the liver. If complement activation proceeds all the way to C5 through C9, forming the membrane attack complex, that causes direct intravascular hemolysis. Clinically, IgM-mediated agglutination in the cold peripheral vessels produces acrocyanosis or Raynaud's phenomenon. One clinical pearl worth remembering: even a low titer of IgM can trigger significant hemolysis because IgM is such an efficient complement activator — one IgM molecule can fix complement, unlike IgG which usually needs two molecules in proximity.

keypoints: Cold AIHA: IgM binds RBCs + C1q in cold peripheral circulation
IgM dissociates centrally; complement cascade continues (C3b, C5b-9)
C3b → extravascular hemolysis (liver); C5b-9/MAC → intravascular hemolysis
Clinical: acrocyanosis/Raynaud's; low IgM titer still hemolyzes
segments.voiceover: Cold AIHA is IgM and complement mediated. IgM binds red cells and fixes C1q in cold peripheral vessels, then dissociates as blood warms, but complement keeps working — C3b drives extravascular hemolysis in the liver, while C5b-9, the membrane attack complex, causes direct intravascular hemolysis. Clinically this produces acrocyanosis or Raynaud's phenomenon, and remember, even a low IgM titer can cause significant hemolysis because one IgM molecule efficiently fixes complement.

This is the master overview slide for autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and the antibody's thermal amplitude is the whole organizing principle. Cold-active antibodies, usually IgM except for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria which is IgG, increase in activity as temperature drops toward zero degrees Celsius and cause intravascular, complement-mediated hemolysis. Warm-active antibodies, usually IgG, are active at body temperature and cause extravascular hemolysis, predominantly in the spleen. Drug-induced AIHA, classically from methyldopa, is clinically and serologically indistinguishable from idiopathic warm AIHA. The serology table is the high-yield memorization target: cold agglutinin disease is 16 to 32 percent of AIHA, occurs in the elderly, DAT shows C3 only, the antibody is IgM with specificity for the I antigen greater than i greater than Pr. Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is about 32 percent of pediatric AIHA, DAT is C3 only, but the antibody is IgG, the Donath-Landsteiner antibody, with anti-P specificity, that IgG-mediated but C3-only DAT pattern is a classic board trap. Warm AIHA is the most common overall at 40 to 70 percent, DAT shows IgG with or without C3, antibody specificity is panagglutinin, rarely anti-Rh. Drug-induced is 12 to 18 percent, with Rh-related, drug-dependent specificity. Clinically, cold agglutinin disease presents with acrocyanosis and livedo reticularis in winter, PCH presents with fever, back or leg pain, and hemoglobinuria after cold exposure, and warm AIHA presents with weakness, dizziness, and hepatosplenomegaly.

keypoints: Cold Ab (usually IgM): active near 0°C, intravascular/complement-mediated hemolysis
Warm Ab (usually IgG): active at 37°C, extravascular hemolysis in spleen
CAD: DAT C3-only, IgM anti-I; PCH: DAT C3-only but IgG Donath-Landsteiner anti-P
Warm AIHA most common (40-70%): DAT IgG±C3, panagglutinin specificity
Drug-induced AIHA (methyldopa) mimics warm AIHA clinically and serologically
segments.voiceover: Organize AIHA by thermal amplitude. Cold antibodies are usually IgM, peak activity near zero degrees, and cause intravascular complement-mediated hemolysis, think cold agglutinin disease with acrocyanosis. Warm antibodies are usually IgG, active at body temperature, and cause extravascular hemolysis in the spleen, this is the most common form overall. Know the DAT trap, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria has an IgG Donath-Landsteiner antibody with anti-P specificity, but the DAT shows only C3, not IgG, because the IgG dissociates at warmer temperatures before testing. Drug-induced AIHA, classically methyldopa, looks just like idiopathic warm AIHA both clinically and serologically.

This table is the classic boards framework for the four mechanisms of drug-induced hemolysis or a positive DAT, and you should be able to name the prototype drug for each. Drug adsorption, or hapten mechanism, prototype drug is penicillin, especially at high doses, the drug binds covalently to the red cell membrane as a cell-bound hapten, and the antibody only reacts with drug-coated cells. DAT is typically IgG-positive, and the clinical course is subacute onset with mild to severe hemolysis. Neoantigen, or immune complex, or ternary complex mechanism, prototype drug is quinidine or stibophen, here the antibody binds the drug-RBC complex together, reacting only when drug is present, DAT is typically complement-only, and the presentation is acute onset with severe hemolysis, this is the mechanism behind sudden brisk intravascular hemolysis with a new drug exposure. Autoimmune mechanism, prototype drug is alpha-methyldopa, the drug induces a truly drug-independent RBC autoantibody, so the antibody is a panagglutinin that reacts even without the drug present, DAT is IgG, and onset is insidious with chronic, mild hemolysis, this is the one that behaves just like idiopathic warm AIHA, which is why methyldopa was highlighted on the previous slide. Finally nonimmune protein adsorption, prototype first-generation cephalosporins, the drug modifies the RBC membrane causing nonspecific protein adsorption, DAT is non-immunoglobulin, and there is no true hemolysis, this is a serologic red herring, a positive DAT without clinical hemolysis.

keypoints: Drug adsorption/hapten (penicillin): drug is cell-bound hapten, Ab reacts only with drug-coated RBCs, IgG DAT
Neoantigen/ternary complex (quinidine): Ab binds drug+RBC together, complement DAT, acute severe hemolysis
Autoimmune (methyldopa): drug induces drug-independent panagglutinin, IgG DAT, insidious chronic hemolysis
Nonimmune adsorption (1st-gen cephalosporins): nonspecific protein adsorption, non-Ig DAT, no hemolysis
segments.voiceover: Four mechanisms, four prototype drugs. Drug adsorption or hapten mechanism is penicillin, the antibody only reacts when drug is stuck to the cell, giving an IgG-positive DAT with subacute hemolysis. Neoantigen or ternary complex mechanism is quinidine, antibody binds drug and red cell together, complement-only DAT, and acute severe intravascular hemolysis. Autoimmune mechanism is methyldopa, the drug triggers a truly drug-independent panagglutinin, IgG DAT, insidious chronic hemolysis identical to warm AIHA. And nonimmune adsorption is first-generation cephalosporins, nonspecific protein sticks to the membrane, DAT is non-immunoglobulin, and importantly there is no actual hemolysis, just a confusing positive DAT.

This diagram walks through the mechanics of the direct and indirect antiglobulin tests, and you need to be crystal clear on what each one actually detects. The direct antiglobulin test, or direct Coombs test, starts with the patient's own red cells, which already have autoantibody bound to them in vivo. You wash the cells, then add anti-human globulin, or AHG, reagent, which is itself an antibody against human IgG or complement. The AHG reagent bridges the antibody-coated red cells together, causing visible agglutination, a positive direct Coombs test therefore tells you the patient's own red cells are coated with antibody or complement in vivo, this is the test you order first when you suspect AIHA. The indirect antiglobulin test works in the opposite direction, you take the patient's serum, which may contain free antibodies, and mix it with reagent red cells of known antigen phenotype. If the serum antibodies bind the reagent cells, adding AHG again causes agglutination. The indirect test detects antibodies circulating in the serum or plasma, or antibodies eluted off a patient's red cells, that's the eluate technique, and this is the test used for antibody screening before transfusion and for identifying antibody specificity in AIHA workups. The key distinction for boards, direct tests the patient's cells, indirect tests the patient's serum or an eluate.

keypoints: DAT (direct Coombs): tests patient RBCs for in-vivo bound Ab/complement, AHG causes agglutination if positive
IAT (indirect Coombs): tests patient serum + reagent RBCs for free circulating antibody
IAT also used to test eluate (antibody stripped off patient RBCs)
AHG reagent = antibody against human IgG/complement, bridges coated RBCs to agglutinate
DAT positive = order first when AIHA suspected; IAT = pretransfusion antibody screen/ID
segments.voiceover: Direct versus indirect antiglobulin test, keep the direction straight. The direct test, or direct Coombs, uses the patient's own red cells, which already carry antibody or complement in vivo, adding anti-human globulin reagent causes agglutination if positive, this is your first test when you suspect AIHA. The indirect test uses patient serum mixed with reagent red cells, detecting free antibody in the serum, or it can test an eluate, antibody stripped off the patient's own cells, and this is the workhorse for pretransfusion antibody screening and specificity identification. Bottom line, direct tests the cells, indirect tests the serum or the eluate.

This slide is a critical technical caveat about the DAT that gets tested on boards. The standard polyspecific direct antiglobulin test can only detect IgG and C3d, that's it, nothing else. Look at the gel card image, the polyspecific reagent shows positive reactions only in the IgG lane and the C3d lane, the IgA and IgM lanes are negative even when those immunoglobulins may be present, because the reagent simply isn't built to catch them. This matters clinically because some AIHA cases are mediated by IgA or IgM alone, and those cases can have a falsely negative or incomplete-looking polyspecific DAT, a classic pitfall, DAT-negative AIHA. When the polyspecific DAT is positive, or when you have high clinical suspicion despite a negative polyspecific test, you escalate to the monospecific direct antiglobulin test, shown in the bottom panel, where you add specific antibodies against each individual component: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3c, C3d, and a control. This lets you determine exactly which immunoglobulin class or complement component is coating the red cells, which in turn narrows the differential, for example IgG-plus-C3d suggests warm AIHA, while C3d alone suggests cold agglutinin disease or PCH. So the workflow is polyspecific DAT to screen, monospecific DAT to characterize.

keypoints: Standard polyspecific DAT detects ONLY IgG and C3d — misses IgA, IgM alone
IgA- or IgM-mediated AIHA can have a falsely negative/unrevealing polyspecific DAT
Monospecific DAT adds individual antisera (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3c, C3d) to pinpoint the coating protein
Monospecific pattern narrows diagnosis: IgG±C3d → warm AIHA; C3d alone → CAD/PCH
segments.voiceover: Know this limitation cold, the standard polyspecific direct antiglobulin test only detects IgG and C3d, it cannot pick up IgA or IgM even if they're coating the red cells. That means rare IgA- or IgM-mediated AIHA can look falsely negative on a routine DAT. When you need more detail, or when the standard DAT doesn't explain the clinical picture, you run the monospecific DAT, testing individually for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3c, and C3d, which tells you precisely what's coating the cells and helps distinguish warm AIHA from cold agglutinin disease or paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria.

This table matches DAT and indirect antiglobulin test reaction patterns to specific diagnoses, and it's a favorite board format, given the pattern, name the disease. First, hemolytic anemia with a negative DAT, this can still be immune-mediated, from IgA or IgM autoantibodies the standard test misses, or simply too few antibody molecules or low-affinity antibody below the detection threshold. Second, hemolytic anemia with negative DAT but positive indirect antiglobulin test, this points to an alloantibody, circulating in serum but not yet bound densely enough to the patient's own cells to give a positive direct test, think delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. Third, hemolytic anemia with both DAT and indirect test positive, and here you split by the DAT reaction pattern. If the pattern is IgG plus-or-minus C3d, think warm-antibody AIHA, or rarely drug-immune hemolytic anemia via the hapten or autoantibody type. If the pattern is C3d alone, without IgG, think warm AIHA with sub-threshold IgG deposition below IgG detection, or the big three cold-mediated conditions, cold agglutinin disease, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria with its Donath-Landsteiner antibody, or drug-immune hemolytic anemia via the ternary complex type. That C3d-alone pattern is the unifying serologic signature of cold-antibody disease.

keypoints: DAT-negative hemolytic anemia: consider IgA/IgM-mediated or too-few/low-affinity autoantibody
DAT-negative, IAT-positive: think alloantibody (e.g., delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction)
DAT+/IAT+ with IgG±C3d: warm AIHA, or rare drug-immune hapten/autoantibody type
DAT+/IAT+ with C3d alone: CAD, PCH (Donath-Landsteiner), or drug-immune ternary complex type
segments.voiceover: This is a pattern-recognition table for boards. DAT-negative hemolytic anemia still may be immune, from IgA or IgM antibodies the test can't catch, or too little antibody to detect. DAT-negative but indirect-test-positive points to an alloantibody, like a delayed transfusion reaction. When both are positive, the DAT reaction pattern is the key, IgG with or without C3d means warm AIHA. C3d alone, without IgG, is the signature of cold-mediated disease, cold agglutinin disease, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, or the ternary complex type of drug-immune hemolytic anemia.

This slide maps out the therapeutic landscape for AIHA, and while boards won't expect encyclopedic drug knowledge, they will expect you to know first-line therapy and the general concept of where newer agents act. First-line for warm AIHA remains corticosteroids, with IVIG and splenectomy as classic second-line options, since warm AIHA is driven by extravascular destruction in the spleen via Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis, splenectomy makes physiologic sense. Beyond that, the pathway breaks into several targetable nodes worth recognizing by category rather than memorizing every name. B-cell directed therapy, rituximab, an anti-CD20 antibody, is the classic steroid-sparing, second-line agent you should know cold, alongside newer agents like ibrutinib, a BTK inhibitor, and BAFF inhibitors. Plasma-cell directed therapy targets the antibody-producing cells directly, bortezomib and daratumumab. Complement inhibition is a major growing category, sutimlimab targets C1 and is FDA-approved specifically for cold agglutinin disease, since cold AIHA is complement-driven, while eculizumab targets C5, more familiar from PNH. FcRn blockers like nipocalimab are a newer mechanism, they accelerate degradation of circulating IgG antibody. And supportive measures matter too, folate supplementation for the chronic hemolysis, and EPO or luspatercept to support marrow compensation. The big picture for boards, warm AIHA equals steroids plus splenectomy plus rituximab, cold agglutinin disease equals complement inhibition with sutimlimab.

keypoints: First-line warm AIHA: corticosteroids; second-line: rituximab (anti-CD20), IVIG, splenectomy
Complement inhibitors: sutimlimab (C1) FDA-approved for cold agglutinin disease; eculizumab (C5)
Plasma-cell/B-cell directed agents: bortezomib, daratumumab, ibrutinib, BAFF inhibitors
FcRn blockers (e.g., nipocalimab) accelerate clearance of circulating IgG
Splenectomy targets extravascular (spleen/ADCC) clearance in warm AIHA
segments.voiceover: For boards, anchor on first-line therapy. Warm AIHA is treated with corticosteroids first, then rituximab, IVIG, or splenectomy as steroid-sparing or refractory options, splenectomy works because warm AIHA destruction happens mainly in the spleen. Cold agglutinin disease is complement-driven, so sutimlimab, a C1 inhibitor, is now FDA-approved specifically for it, while eculizumab blocks C5. Other categories to recognize by class include B-cell and plasma-cell directed agents like ibrutinib and daratumumab, and newer FcRn blockers that speed up clearance of pathogenic IgG. Don't forget supportive care, folate and agents that boost marrow compensation.

This algorithm walks through management of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, stratified by symptom severity. Asymptomatic patients just get observation and folate. Symptomatic non-severe disease, hemoglobin 6 to 10, tolerated anemia, moves straight to oral prednisone, 1 to 1.5 milligrams per kilogram per day, for 3 to 4 weeks. For severe disease, hemoglobin under 6 with instability, add IV methylprednisolone 100 to 200 milligrams a day, plus or minus transfusion and IVIG, before converging on that same oral steroid course. Good responders get a slow taper, 10 milligrams a week down to 0.5 per kilogram per day, then 5 milligrams a day until off, over 3 to 6 months, and you hold the taper if hemoglobin drops below 10 with active hemolysis. For poor response or relapse, look for a secondary cause first and treat it. If there is no secondary cause, that is when second line therapy kicks in, rituximab or splenectomy are the go-to options, with steroid sparing agents like cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, MMF, or azathioprine as alternatives, and consider prophylactic LMWH given the known thrombosis risk in AIHA. For very severe disease with no response within a week, escalate early to rituximab plus or minus plasma exchange.

keypoints: First line: PO prednisone 1-1.5 mg/kg/d x 3-4 wk
Severe (Hb<6): add IV methylprednisolone ± transfusion/IVIG
Poor response, no 2° cause → rituximab or splenectomy
Taper: 10mg/wk → 0.5mg/kg/d → 5mg/d over 3-6 mo
Consider LMWH prophylaxis (AIHA = high VTE risk)
segments.voiceover: For warm AIHA, first line is oral prednisone, 1 to 1.5 milligrams per kilogram daily for 3 to 4 weeks, with IV methylprednisolone added for severe unstable disease. If there is poor response and no secondary cause, second line means rituximab or splenectomy, tapering steroids slowly over 3 to 6 months once there is a good response. Do not forget VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, since AIHA carries a significant clotting risk.

Cold agglutinin disease management starts with general measures for everyone, treat any secondary cause like infection, lymphoma, or autoimmune disease, avoid cold exposure by keeping the extremities warm, and always pre-warm blood products and IV fluids to prevent triggering hemolysis. Asymptomatic patients just need observation, supportive care, and folate. For symptomatic CAD, first line is rituximab, 375 milligrams per meter squared weekly for 4 weeks, with a response rate around 50 percent. Second line options push that response rate higher, rituximab combined with fludarabine or bendamustine gets response rates over 70 percent, and sutimlimab, a C1 inhibitor, was FDA approved in February 2022, giving rapid onset with a 54 percent response rate. For emergencies, you are looking at blood transfusion with an in-line warmer, plasma exchange, or the C5 inhibitor eculizumab. Unlike warm AIHA where steroids are first line, steroids are notably ineffective in CAD because it is an IgM mediated, complement driven process rather than an IgG mediated one. Also remember, consider LMWH prophylaxis in untreated patients with severe anemia or additional thrombotic risk factors.

keypoints: 1st line: Rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly x4wk (RR ~50%)
2nd line: R + fludarabine/bendamustine (RR 70%+)
Sutimlimab (C1 inhibitor): rapid onset, RR 54%, FDA 2022
Steroids largely ineffective in CAD (unlike warm AIHA)
Always pre-warm blood products/fluids; avoid cold exposure
segments.voiceover: For cold agglutinin disease, first line is rituximab monotherapy with about a 50 percent response rate. Second line escalates to rituximab plus fludarabine or bendamustine for response rates over 70 percent, or sutimlimab, a C1 inhibitor approved in 2022 that works fast. Key exam point, steroids do not work well in CAD, unlike warm AIHA, because this is complement mediated IgM disease. And always keep patients warm and pre-warm any transfused blood.

This is the classic red cell membrane cytoskeleton diagram, and it is high yield because the two types of protein interactions map directly onto two different diseases. Vertical interactions connect the lipid bilayer to the underlying spectrin cytoskeleton, via band 3, ankyrin, and protein 4.2 on one axis, and glycophorin C with protein 4.1R on the other. When vertical interactions fail, the membrane destabilizes, buds off, and you get spherocytosis. Horizontal interactions are the side to side connections between spectrin dimers, alpha and beta spectrin self associating into tetramers, and connecting through protein 4.1R, actin, and adducin to glycophorin C. When horizontal interactions fail, the cell cannot maintain its shape under shear stress, giving you elliptocytosis. Band 3 anchors the vertical connection to ankyrin and also carries CD47 and Rh proteins, while GPA and GPC are surface glycophorins. The core teaching point for boards, vertical defect equals spherocytosis, horizontal defect equals elliptocytosis.

keypoints: Vertical interactions (band 3-ankyrin-4.2-spectrin) → defect = spherocytosis
Horizontal interactions (spectrin-spectrin, 4.1R-actin) → defect = elliptocytosis
Band 3 anchors bilayer to ankyrin; carries Rh, CD47
α/β spectrin tetramers form the horizontal skeletal lattice
segments.voiceover: Remember this one rule, vertical protein interactions, band 3, ankyrin, protein 4.2, connecting the membrane to the spectrin skeleton, when defective cause spherocytosis. Horizontal interactions, the spectrin-spectrin self association and the 4.1R-actin-adducin complex, when defective cause elliptocytosis. That vertical versus horizontal distinction is the single most testable fact from this diagram.

This table is a board favorite, matching membrane proteins to their disease phenotypes. Ankyrin defects are the most common cause of typical dominant hereditary spherocytosis. Band 3 defects cause HS, but also Southeast Asian ovalocytosis, nonimmune hydrops fetalis, and hereditary acanthocytosis, band 3 HS classically shows pincered spherocytes on the blood film before splenectomy, and SAO results from a specific 9 amino acid deletion. Alpha spectrin defects cause HS, HE, hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, and NIHF, with acanthocytic spherocytes on film, and here the location of the mutation determines the clinical phenotype. Beta spectrin is the most common cause of typical HE, but also causes HS, HPP, and NIHF. Protein 4.2 deficiency causes HS and is notably enriched in Japanese patients with autosomal recessive inheritance, a classic board pearl. Protein 4.1R deficiency causes HE and is found in certain European and Arab populations, and glycophorin C defects cause HE through concomitant protein 4.1 deficiency. High yield associations to memorize, ankyrin and protein 4.2 for HS, especially the Japanese autosomal recessive protein 4.2 link, and beta spectrin for HE.

keypoints: Ankyrin = most common cause of dominant HS
Protein 4.2 deficiency → HS, AR, classic in Japanese patients
β-spectrin mutations = most common cause of typical HE
Band 3 → HS (pincered cells), SAO (9-aa deletion), NIHF, HAc
α-spectrin mutation location determines phenotype (HS/HE/HPP/NIHF)
segments.voiceover: Key protein-disease pairs for boards, ankyrin is the most common cause of dominant hereditary spherocytosis, and protein 4.2 deficiency, causing HS, is classically autosomal recessive and enriched in Japanese patients. Beta spectrin mutations are the most common cause of typical hereditary elliptocytosis. Band 3 defects give you pincered spherocytes in HS, and also cause Southeast Asian ovalocytosis from a 9 amino acid deletion. And remember, alpha spectrin's phenotype depends on exactly where the mutation sits.

This diagram catalogs the abnormal red cell morphologies tied to membrane alterations, and each shape reflects a specific biophysical defect. Target cells reflect an increased surface area to volume ratio, either an absolute increase in phospholipid and cholesterol as in obstructive liver disease, or a relative increase from reduced cell volume, as in iron deficiency, thalassemia, hemoglobin E, or hemoglobin C. Acanthocytes show cholesterol accumulation in the outer leaflet, seen in liver disease, or sphingomyelin accumulation, seen in abetalipoproteinemia. Echinocytes reflect outer bilayer expansion relative to the inner surface, seen in uremia, pyruvate kinase deficiency, or as an artifact. Spherocytes arise from spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3 deficiency causing membrane instability, lipid loss, and a falling MCV, that is hereditary spherocytosis, or from reticuloendothelial removal of antibody coated membrane, that is autoimmune hemolysis. Elliptocytes come from altered horizontal spectrin dimer interactions, the classic mechanism in common HE. Stomatocytes reflect expansion of the inner bilayer surface, seen with vinca alkaloids, alcoholism, or cation permeability disorders. And poikilocytes or fragments reflect severely impaired horizontal protein interactions, as in hemolytic HE or hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, or mechanical causes like microangiopathy or intravascular prosthesis.

keypoints: Target cells: ↑SA:volume — liver disease, Fe deficiency, thalassemia, Hgb E/C
Spherocytes: spectrin/ankyrin/band3 loss → ↓MCV (HS or AIHA)
Elliptocytes: altered horizontal spectrin-dimer interaction (HE)
Acanthocytes: cholesterol accumulation (liver dz, abetalipoproteinemia)
Echinocytes: uremia, PK deficiency, or artifact
segments.voiceover: Match the shape to the mechanism. Target cells mean increased surface to volume ratio, think liver disease or iron deficiency and thalassemia. Spherocytes come from spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3 loss, either hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolysis stripping the membrane. Elliptocytes reflect impaired horizontal spectrin interactions, the hallmark of hereditary elliptocytosis. Acanthocytes point to liver disease or abetalipoproteinemia, and echinocytes to uremia or PK deficiency.

Hereditary spherocytosis is your classic membrane disorder for boards. Most cases are autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive inheritance occurs with protein 4.2 and alpha spectrin defects, that is a testable exception. The defective proteins are ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2, and spectrin, with ankyrin being the most common culprit overall. Clinically it presents with hemolytic anemia, intermittent jaundice, splenomegaly, and pigment gallstones leading to cholecystitis. For diagnosis, the classic tests are osmotic fragility and, increasingly favored now, the EMA binding test, which measures band 3 by flow cytometry and has largely replaced osmotic fragility as the preferred screening test. Treatment is splenectomy, folic acid supplementation, and transfusion as needed. Mechanistically, spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, or protein 4.2 deficiency destabilizes the vertical membrane connections, the cell releases microvesicles and loses surface area faster than volume, forming spherocytes. These get trapped in the spleen, where low pH and macrophage contact drive further membrane loss, creating microspherocytes and hemolysis, a vicious cycle of splenic conditioning.

keypoints: Most AD; AR forms: protein 4.2, α-spectrin
Ankyrin = most common defect; also band 3, protein 4.2, spectrin
Diagnosis: EMA binding (band 3) test — preferred over osmotic fragility
Triad: hemolytic anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly + pigment gallstones
Treatment: splenectomy, folic acid, transfusion
segments.voiceover: Hereditary spherocytosis is mostly autosomal dominant, with protein 4.2 and alpha spectrin defects as the autosomal recessive exceptions. Ankyrin is the most commonly defective protein. The board favorite diagnostic test now is EMA binding, which has surpassed osmotic fragility. Clinically expect hemolytic anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and pigment gallstones, and treatment centers on splenectomy plus folic acid.

Two membrane screening tests worth knowing cold. The EMA binding test is flow cytometry based. Eosin-5-maleimide dye binds covalently to band 3 protein on intact red cells, and you measure fluorescence intensity. Decreased fluorescence means less band 3, or less membrane surface area, which points you toward hereditary spherocytosis. Then the osmotic fragility curve. Plot hemolysis percent against sodium chloride concentration. A left-shifted curve means increased fragility, which comes from a decreased surface area to volume ratio, the classic spherocyte shape. That's your hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and sometimes hereditary elliptocytosis, though HE can be normal to increased. A right-shifted curve means decreased fragility, from an increased surface area to volume ratio, seen with target cells or stomatocytes. Think thalassemia, iron deficiency anemia, and liver disease, all conditions that give the red cell extra membrane relative to its volume, making it resistant to osmotic lysis.

keypoints: EMA binding test: ↓ fluorescence → ↓ band 3 → think HS
↑ Osmotic fragility (left shift): ↓ SA:volume → spherocytes → HS, AIHA
↓ Osmotic fragility (right shift): ↑ SA:volume → target cells/stomatocytes
Right-shift causes: thalassemia, iron deficiency anemia, liver disease
segments.voiceover: Quick recap. EMA binding tests band 3 directly, low fluorescence suggests HS. On the osmotic fragility curve, a left shift means increased fragility from a low surface area to volume ratio, that's the spherocyte pattern in HS and AIHA. A right shift means decreased fragility from a high surface area to volume ratio, that's your target cell and stomatocyte pattern, seen in thalassemia, iron deficiency, and liver disease.

This is the metabolic map of the red cell, and boards love testing the two branch points. The main trunk is anaerobic glycolysis, the Embden-Meyerhof pathway, which generates ATP and 2,3-DPG and is where pyruvate kinase, PK, sits near the bottom. A side branch off glucose-6-phosphate is the hexose monophosphate shunt, driven by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, G6PD. This shunt generates NADPH, which feeds glutathione metabolism, the cell's main antioxidant defense system. When G6PD activity is low, the cell can't regenerate reduced glutathione fast enough under oxidative stress, hemoglobin denatures and precipitates as Heinz bodies, and you get a hemolytic crisis. Contrast that with the glycolytic pathway defects, like pyruvate kinase deficiency, which have variable clinical significance and, importantly, no characteristic morphologic findings on the smear, unlike G6PD deficiency where you can catch Heinz bodies during a crisis. So the exam distinction is: HMP shunt defect equals oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies, glycolytic defect equals chronic hemolysis without a specific morphologic clue.

keypoints: HMP shunt (G6PD) → NADPH → glutathione → antioxidant defense
↓G6PD/GSH + oxidative stress → Heinz bodies → hemolytic crisis
Glycolysis (PK) → ATP, 2,3-DPG; PK deficiency = variable severity, no characteristic smear finding
G6PD and PK are the two classic RBC enzymopathies
segments.voiceover: Two enzymes to anchor this slide. G6PD drives the hexose monophosphate shunt, making NADPH to keep glutathione reduced, your antioxidant shield. Deficiency leads to Heinz bodies and hemolytic crisis under oxidative stress. Pyruvate kinase drives glycolysis, making ATP, and its deficiency causes hemolysis of variable severity but with no specific smear finding to point to. That contrast, oxidative versus energy-deficiency hemolysis, is the key takeaway.

G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive, gene at Xq28, thirteen exons, and there are over four hundred described variant enzymes, making it the most common red cell enzyme disease worldwide, capable of causing both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis. The WHO classification is built entirely around residual enzyme activity. Class I is severe, under ten percent activity, and rare, but it's the one that causes chronic hemolysis even without a trigger. Class II is also severe, under ten percent, common in Mediterranean and Asian populations, and causes intermittent hemolysis. Variants here include Mediterranean, Kaiping, Gaohe, and Chinese-3. Class III is moderate, ten to sixty percent activity, seen in Africa and Southeast Asia, causing intermittent hemolysis only under stress. This includes the A- variant, found in about ten percent of Africans, and the Canton variant. Class IV has near normal activity, sixty to one-fifty percent, no hemolysis, the wild-type B and A+ variants. Class V is over one-fifty percent activity, essentially no clinical relevance. For boards with a Taiwan or Asian population focus, remember Canton, a G1376T mutation, accounts for about fifty percent of G6PD deficient Taiwanese males, with Kaiping second at roughly twenty-one percent.

keypoints: X-linked recessive, Xq28, >400 variants — most common RBC enzymopathy
Class I: <10% activity, rare, chronic hemolysis even without trigger
Class II: <10% activity, Mediterranean/Asian, intermittent hemolysis
Class III: 10-60% activity, African A- and Canton, stress-triggered hemolysis
Canton variant most common in Taiwanese males (~50%)
segments.voiceover: Bottom line for boards. G6PD deficiency is X-linked, Xq28, the most common red cell enzymopathy. Class I is rare but causes chronic hemolysis with under ten percent activity. Class II, also under ten percent, causes intermittent hemolysis and includes the Mediterranean and Kaiping variants. Class III is moderate, ten to sixty percent activity, includes African A- and the Canton variant, and only hemolyzes under stress. Classes IV and V have normal or increased activity and no disease. In Taiwan, Canton is the dominant variant.

This is the drug and chemical list for G6PD deficiency, and you don't need to memorize every entry, you need to recognize the pattern and a few named agents. These are all oxidant stressors, unsafe for WHO class I, II, and III variants because those patients can't regenerate reduced glutathione fast enough to buffer the oxidative load. The classic named agents worth knowing are primaquine, the antimalarial that's a textbook trigger question, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, sulfa drugs like sulfacetamide, sulfanilamide, and sulfapyridine, and of course fava beans, which give you favism, most severe in the Mediterranean and Kaiping variants. The one highlighted in red here, and clinically the most important for an inpatient hematology consult, is urate oxidase, rasburicase, used for tumor lysis syndrome. Giving rasburicase to a G6PD deficient patient can trigger severe, even fatal, hemolysis, so screening G6PD status before starting rasburicase is standard practice, especially in patients of African, Mediterranean, or Asian descent. On the safe side, acetaminophen, aspirin, and ascorbic acid are fine to use.

keypoints: Classic oxidant triggers: primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, fava beans
Rasburicase (urate oxidase) — screen G6PD before giving for tumor lysis syndrome
Rasburicase-induced hemolysis can be severe/fatal in deficient patients
Safe: acetaminophen, aspirin, ascorbic acid
segments.voiceover: The high-yield drug list boils down to a few names. Primaquine, dapsone, sulfa drugs, nitrofurantoin, and fava beans are classic oxidant triggers you should recognize instantly. The one most likely to show up as a clinical vignette is rasburicase, given for tumor lysis syndrome, which can cause severe hemolysis in G6PD deficient patients, so screening before use matters. Acetaminophen, aspirin, and ascorbic acid remain safe choices.

Clinically, G6PD deficiency presents as acute hemolytic anemia and, in newborns, neonatal jaundice. When you're asked what precipitates hemolysis, the answer boards want is infection, that's actually the most common trigger, more common than drugs. Other precipitants are certain drugs, diabetic acidosis, and fava beans, particularly relevant in Mediterranean and Asian variants where favism is classic. For diagnosis, you screen with the fluorescent spot test and confirm with quantitative spectrophotometric analysis measuring actual enzyme activity. Two testing pitfalls are frequently tested. First, testing during or immediately after acute hemolysis can be falsely negative, because the older, more enzyme-deficient red cells have already been destroyed, leaving a population of young cells and reticulocytes that have relatively higher G6PD activity, so you need to retest weeks later. Second, female heterozygotes can be difficult to diagnose because of X-chromosome mosaicism, or lyonization, meaning they have a mixed population of normal and deficient red cells that can average out to a falsely normal result. Treatment is supportive: remove the offending oxidant, give folic acid, and transfuse if the anemia is severe.

keypoints: Infection = most common hemolysis trigger (more than drugs)
Screen: fluorescent spot test; confirm: quantitative spectrophotometry
Testing during acute hemolysis can be falsely negative — retest later
Female heterozygotes: falsely normal due to X-inactivation mosaicism (lyonization)
Treatment: remove trigger, folic acid, transfusion if severe
segments.voiceover: Remember infection, not drugs, is the number one hemolysis trigger in G6PD deficiency. Diagnosis starts with a fluorescent spot test and is confirmed by quantitative spectrophotometry. Two classic pitfalls: testing right after an acute hemolytic episode can give a false negative because the deficient cells are already gone, and female heterozygotes can look falsely normal due to X-inactivation mosaicism. Management is supportive, remove the trigger, give folic acid, and transfuse if needed.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is fundamentally different from the enzyme defects we just covered, it's an acquired clonal stem cell disorder, not inherited. A somatic mutation in the PIG-A gene, which sits on the X chromosome but is acquired in a hematopoietic stem cell, not germline, knocks out biosynthesis of the GPI anchor, the glycophosphatidylinositol structure that tethers certain proteins to the red cell membrane. Without a functional GPI anchor, the cell loses two critical complement regulatory proteins: CD55, also called decay accelerating factor or DAF, which normally inhibits C3 and C5 convertase, and CD59, also called MIRL, membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis, which normally blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex, C5b-9. Without these brakes, the alternative complement pathway runs unchecked on the red cell surface, generating C5a and driving formation of the MAC, which punches holes in the membrane and causes intravascular hemolysis, classically presenting with hemoglobinuria, often worse overnight or on first-void morning urine. This complement biology is exactly why eculizumab, which binds and blocks cleavage of C5, is the targeted treatment, it stops MAC formation right at that terminal step.

keypoints: Acquired somatic PIG-A mutation (X-linked gene) → loss of GPI anchor
Lose CD55/DAF (blocks C3/C5 convertase) and CD59/MIRL (blocks MAC)
Unchecked alternative complement pathway → intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria
Eculizumab = anti-C5 antibody, blocks membrane attack complex formation
segments.voiceover: Key facts for PNH. It's an acquired, not inherited, somatic mutation in PIG-A, which knocks out the GPI anchor. That means loss of CD55, DAF, and CD59, MIRL, the two complement regulators normally protecting the red cell. Without them, unchecked alternative pathway complement activation causes intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Eculizumab targets C5 directly, blocking formation of the membrane attack complex, and is the standard targeted therapy.

Let's talk about how we actually diagnose PNH in the lab. The classic older tests are the acid Ham test and the sucrose lysis test, or sugar water test, both of which lyse PNH red cells that have been exposed to activated complement. They're cheap, but they're labor intensive, insensitive, and not quantitative, so they're basically obsolete for board purposes. The modern gold standard is flow cytometry, which detects loss of GPI anchored proteins. On red cells you look at CD59 and CD55, and CD59 is actually better for distinguishing type two from type three PNH clones. On granulocytes you use CD59, CD55, CD24, CD16, and FLAER, which stands for fluorescently labeled inactive toxin aerolysin. FLAER binds directly to the GPI anchor itself, so it's more robust for clone size estimation, especially in granulocytes, because red cell measurements can underestimate clone size due to hemolysis. A key testable point, you need at least two antibodies to confirm the diagnosis, not just one, because CD59 and CD55 have different relative intensities on different cell lines, CD59 is brighter than CD55 on red cells, but dimmer than CD55 on white cells.

keypoints: Flow cytometry (CD59/CD55/FLAER) = gold standard, not Ham/sucrose lysis
Need ≥2 GPI-linked markers to confirm diagnosis
FLAER binds GPI anchor directly → best for clone size
CD59 > CD55 intensity on RBC; CD59 < CD55 on WBC
CD59 better distinguishes type II vs III clones
segments.voiceover: For boards, remember flow cytometry using GPI anchored proteins is the diagnostic gold standard for PNH, replacing the old Ham and sucrose lysis tests. You always need at least two antibodies, commonly CD59 and CD55, because their relative intensity flips between cell types, CD59 is brighter on red cells while CD55 is brighter on white cells. FLAER, which binds the GPI anchor directly, is the most robust marker for estimating clone size, particularly on granulocytes, since red cell based estimates tend to underestimate true clone size from ongoing hemolysis.

This slide illustrates PNH mosaicism, which is a high yield concept. Patients don't have a single uniform population of abnormal cells, instead they have a mosaic of type one cells which are normal, type two cells with partial PIGA deficiency and partial loss of GPI anchored proteins, and type three cells with complete PIGA deficiency and complete loss. The proportion of type three cells drives the clinical picture, a patient dominated by type three cells has high grade intravascular hemolysis, while a patient with mostly type one and only a small type three population has minimal hemolysis. This mosaicism is also dynamic and can shift over time. The table on the right, from a study of eighty PNH patients, shows how varied the presentation can be, symptoms of anemia in about a third, hemoglobinuria in about a quarter, and thrombosis or embolism in only six percent, even though thrombosis is the most feared and lethal complication. Aplastic anemia features in thirteen percent, reflecting the close relationship between PNH and bone marrow failure syndromes. The takeaway for boards, don't expect classic hemoglobinuria in every PNH patient, presentation is heterogeneous and clone size correlates with hemolytic severity.

keypoints: Type I = normal, II = partial PIGA deficiency, III = complete PIGA deficiency
% type III clone correlates with hemolysis severity
PNH clone size is dynamic, changes over time
Only ~26% present with hemoglobinuria; only 6% with thrombosis
13% present as aplastic anemia — PNH/AA overlap
segments.voiceover: Key testable point, PNH cells come in three flow cytometry types, type one is normal, type two has partial PIGA gene deficiency, and type three has complete deficiency with no GPI anchored proteins at all. The percentage of type three cells determines how severe the hemolysis is. Clinical presentation is heterogeneous, only about a quarter of patients present with classic hemoglobinuria, while thirteen percent present as aplastic anemia, highlighting the tight link between PNH and bone marrow failure. Clone size can also change dynamically over time, so a single measurement doesn't capture the full picture.

This is the complement cascade slide, and you need to know exactly where each PNH drug acts. Complement can be activated through three pathways, classical, lectin, or alternative, and all three converge on C3 convertase. The alternative pathway is constitutively active, ticking over C3 to C3b, which is why PNH red cells, lacking the protective proteins CD55 and CD59, are especially vulnerable. In the proximal pathway, Iptacopan inhibits Factor B and Danicopan inhibits Factor D, both blocking formation of the C3 convertase from the alternative pathway side. CD55, the protein missing in PNH, normally accelerates decay of that convertase. Pegcetacoplan inhibits C3 itself, blocking cleavage into C3a and C3b, which shuts down both the proximal amplification loop and downstream C5 convertase formation. Moving to the terminal pathway, C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b, and C5b combines with C6 through C9 to form the membrane attack complex, which is what CD59 normally blocks. The terminal C5 inhibitors, eculizumab, ravulizumab, and crovalimab, all block this step, preventing intravascular hemolysis but not extravascular hemolysis, since C3b opsonization upstream is untouched. Investigational agents target MASP-3, Factor D, Factor H, and C3 as well.

keypoints: C5 inhibitors (eculizumab/ravulizumab/crovalimab) block MAC, mimic CD59
C3/proximal inhibitors (pegcetacoplan, iptacopan, danicopan) block upstream, mimic CD55/CFB/CFD
C5 inhibitors stop IVH but not EVH (C3b opsonization persists)
Alternative pathway is constitutively active — why PNH RBCs are vulnerable
Proximal inhibition addresses breakthrough EVH on C5 inhibitors
segments.voiceover: For boards, map the drugs to their targets. Terminal C5 inhibitors, eculizumab, ravulizumab, and crovalimab, block the membrane attack complex, essentially replacing the function of CD59, and they control intravascular hemolysis but not extravascular hemolysis. Proximal inhibitors act further upstream, iptacopan blocks Factor B, danicopan blocks Factor D, and pegcetacoplan blocks C3 directly, replacing the function of CD55. These proximal agents control both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis, which matters clinically for patients with breakthrough extravascular hemolysis while on a C5 inhibitor.

This slide defines classical PNH and its treatment algorithm, which is very testable. Classical PNH is diagnosed when the PNH clone exceeds thirty to fifty percent, plus symptomatic hemolysis with hemoglobin under seven to nine requiring transfusion, thromboembolism including any arterial clot or a venous clot with organ damage, or renal impairment with rising creatinine over two. Management splits into supportive care and anti-complement therapy. Supportive care includes folate and iron, leukoreduced transfusions, and meningococcal vaccination before starting a C5 inhibitor, since these patients risk meningococcal sepsis, plus pneumococcal and Hemophilus vaccines for proximal inhibitors. Full dose anticoagulation treats established thromboembolism, and prophylaxis is considered in high risk untreated patients. Anti-complement therapy includes terminal C5 inhibitors, eculizumab, ravulizumab, and crovalimab, which target intravascular hemolysis, and proximal inhibitors, pegcetacoplan against C3, and iptacopan or danicopan against the alternative pathway, which cover both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis. If anemia persists on a C5 inhibitor, think of four causes, underlying bone marrow failure, a C5 polymorphism causing resistance, breakthrough intravascular hemolysis from triggers or subtherapeutic levels, or extravascular hemolysis with a positive C3d DAT, which should prompt switching to proximal inhibition.

keypoints: Classical PNH: clone >30-50% + symptomatic hemolysis/thrombosis/renal impairment
Meningococcal vaccine mandatory before C5 inhibitors (± pneumococcal/HiB for proximal)
C5 inhibitors control IVH only; C3/proximal inhibitors control IVH + EVH
Residual anemia on C5i: marrow failure, C5 polymorphism, breakthrough IVH, or EVH (C3d+ DAT)
Full-dose anticoagulation for established thromboembolism
segments.voiceover: High yield board points here. Classical PNH treatment is triggered by a clone over thirty to fifty percent with symptomatic hemolysis, thromboembolism, or renal impairment. Always give meningococcal vaccination before starting a C5 inhibitor. Remember that C5 inhibitors only control intravascular hemolysis, while proximal C3 or alternative pathway inhibitors cover both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis. And if a patient has residual anemia on a C5 inhibitor, work through four causes, bone marrow failure, a C5 polymorphism, breakthrough intravascular hemolysis, or extravascular hemolysis marked by a positive C3d DAT.

This is a dense but high yield reference table on causes of macrocytosis, defined as MCV over ninety seven, with a column showing likelihood of MCV over one hundred ten for each cause. The highest yield causes with high likelihood of a very elevated MCV are cobalamin or folate deficiency, cytotoxic or immunosuppressive drugs, antiviral drugs, aplastic anemia or pure red cell aplasia, and as a lab artifact, cold agglutinins or severe hyperglycemia falsely elevating the measured MCV. Moderate likelihood causes include alcohol with or without liver disease, myelodysplastic syndrome, copper deficiency anemia, reticulocytosis from hemolytic anemia, and non-alcoholic liver disease. Low likelihood causes include anticonvulsants, myeloproliferative disease or leukemia, sideroblastic anemia, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, chronic lung disease or smoking, and multiple myeloma. The key testable pattern for boards, when you see a truly massive MCV, well above one hundred ten, your differential should narrow sharply toward B12 or folate deficiency, myelosuppressive or antiviral drug effects, aplastic anemia, or a spurious lab artifact like cold agglutinins or hyperglycemia, rather than the more common but milder causes like alcohol or hypothyroidism.

keypoints: Macrocytosis = MCV >97 fL
MCV >110 fL → think B12/folate deficiency, cytotoxic/antiviral drugs, aplastic anemia
Cold agglutinins & severe hyperglycemia = artifactual (spurious) macrocytosis
Moderate causes: alcohol, MDS, copper deficiency, reticulocytosis, liver disease
Low likelihood: hypothyroidism, pregnancy, smoking, myeloma
segments.voiceover: For boards, remember that a very high MCV, well above one hundred ten, points to a short list of high likelihood causes, cobalamin or folate deficiency, cytotoxic or antiviral drugs, and aplastic anemia or pure red cell aplasia. Also remember the artifact category, cold agglutinins and severe hyperglycemia can spuriously elevate the measured MCV without true macrocytosis. Milder or more moderate elevations are more often from alcohol, liver disease, myelodysplastic syndrome, or ongoing reticulocytosis from hemolysis.

This slide covers folate and cobalamin physiology, explaining why their deficiencies behave so differently clinically. Folate is absorbed in the duodenum and ileum, with typical intake around two hundred micrograms a day. Body folate stores are small, only five to ten milligrams, and since daily losses run one to two percent of that store, depletion can occur within just three to six months of poor intake, which is why folate deficiency develops quickly, for example with alcoholism or poor diet. Cobalamin works differently, it binds intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Total body B12 content is about two point five milligrams, but daily loss is only about one microgram, so depletion takes three to four years even with zero intake, which is why B12 deficiency from strict veganism takes years to manifest, while gastric or ileal disease causes it faster by blocking absorption. B12 is found in fish, animal products, milk, eggs, and cheese, but essentially absent from plants. Both vitamins converge on the folate regeneration cycle in the bone marrow, feeding thymidylate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase to support DNA synthesis in erythroblasts, which is why deficiency of either one produces the same megaloblastic, macrocytic picture.

keypoints: Folate: absorbed duodenum/ileum; store 5-10mg; depletion in 3-6 months
B12: needs intrinsic factor, absorbed in terminal ileum; store 2.5mg; depletion in 3-4 years
B12 in animal products only — vegans at risk without supplementation
Both feed folate regeneration cycle → same megaloblastic/macrocytic picture
Slow B12 depletion (years) explains delayed onset of deficiency
segments.voiceover: Key contrast for boards, folate stores are small and deplete in just three to six months of poor intake, so folate deficiency shows up fast. B12 stores are much larger relative to daily loss, so depletion from dietary lack alone takes three to four years, though malabsorption from gastric or ileal disease works faster. B12 requires intrinsic factor and ileal absorption, and it's found only in animal products, so vegans need supplementation. Both vitamins feed the same folate regeneration cycle for DNA synthesis, which is why either deficiency causes megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia.

Megaloblastic anemia is fundamentally a disorder of impaired DNA synthesis, most often driven by vitamin B12, or cobalamin, deficiency. The classic lab pattern you need cold for boards is a low cobalamin level with elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, an MCV greater than 110 femtoliters, and evidence of ineffective erythropoiesis, meaning pancytopenia, a markedly elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and a low haptoglobin, which together mimic hemolysis even though the real problem is destruction of cells within the marrow. Remember that methylmalonic acid is elevated only in B12 deficiency, not folate deficiency, which is the key distinguishing test. Causes of B12 deficiency to know include pernicious anemia, which involves autoantibodies against parietal cells or intrinsic factor and is classically diagnosed with the Schilling test, as well as gastrectomy, chronic pancreatitis, small bowel bacterial overgrowth, ileitis or ileal resection, and intestinal parasites such as fish tapeworm. On smear, look for panmyelosis, megaloblasts, giant bands, macro-ovalocytes, and hypersegmented neutrophils, which are the single most recognizable clue on a board exam image. Management is replacement with cyanocobalamin, typically 1000 micrograms intramuscularly for the first several weeks, transitioning to a low oral dose if intestinal absorption is intact.

keypoints: MCV >110 fL plus hypersegmented neutrophils = megaloblastic
B12 deficiency uniquely raises methylmalonic acid, not just homocysteine
Pernicious anemia: anti-parietal cell / anti-IF antibodies
Ineffective erythropoiesis mimics hemolysis: ↑LDH, ↑indirect bili, ↓haptoglobin
Treat with IM cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg initially
segments.voiceover: For boards, remember MCV over 110 with hypersegmented neutrophils screams megaloblastic anemia. The key differentiator from folate deficiency is an elevated methylmalonic acid, which only rises with B12 deficiency. Pernicious anemia is caused by antibodies against parietal cells or intrinsic factor. Because turnover in the marrow is so ineffective, you'll see a pseudo-hemolytic picture with high LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and low haptoglobin. Treatment starts with intramuscular cyanocobalamin, one thousand micrograms.

Aplastic anemia is defined by pancytopenia with fatty replacement of the marrow and a near absence of hematopoietic precursors.
