It's rare, with an incidence of about two per million per year, and has a bimodal age distribution, peaking at fifteen to twenty five years and again at sixty five to sixty nine. Diagnosis requires marrow cellularity below twenty five percent, or below fifty percent if fewer than thirty percent of the remaining cells are hematopoietic. Cytogenetics are usually normal in true aplastic anemia, though you can see six p uniparental disomy in about thirteen percent, and low rates of minus seven or del seven q, plus eight, and minus thirteen q. Severity grading is the classic board question: severe aplastic anemia requires at least two of a reticulocyte count under twenty thousand or under one percent corrected, an absolute neutrophil count under five hundred, and a platelet count under twenty thousand, while very severe aplastic anemia is defined by an ANC under two hundred. The table contrasting hypocellular MDS with aplastic anemia is high yield. Aplastic anemia tends to be bimodal in age, has normal cytogenetics, a PNH clone in twenty to thirty percent of patients, absent blasts, only erythroid dysplasia, and absent or low variant allele frequency somatic mutations without splicing mutations. Hypocellular MDS instead occurs in older patients, has abnormal cytogenetics about half the time, no PNH clone, normal to increased blasts, trilineage or bilineage dysplasia, and canonical MDS mutations including spliceosomal genes. Features specific for MDS over aplastic anemia include dysgranulopoiesis, dysmegakaryopoiesis, and ringed sideroblasts.

keypoints: Severe AA: ≥2 of ANC<500, plt<20k, retic<20k/<1%
Very severe AA: ANC <200
Bimodal peaks: age 15-25 and 65-69
PNH clone 20-30% supports AA over primary MDS
MDS-specific clues: dysgranulopoiesis, dysmegakaryopoiesis, ringed sideroblasts
segments.voiceover: Know the severity cutoffs cold: severe aplastic anemia needs at least two of an ANC under five hundred, platelets under twenty thousand, or a corrected reticulocyte under one percent, and very severe means the ANC drops below two hundred. Peak incidence is bimodal, young adults and the elderly. A PNH clone favors aplastic anemia over primary hypocellular MDS, while dysgranulopoiesis, dysmegakaryopoiesis, and ringed sideroblasts point you toward MDS instead.

About thirty percent of aplastic anemia patients carry MDS-related somatic mutations, and knowing which ones predict which outcome is a favorite board pearl. Mutations in PIGA, BCOR, or BCORL1 are considered favorable, they're associated with a better response to immunosuppressive therapy and better overall survival, and biologically they make sense since BCOR and BCORL1 mutations are thought to arise in the same clonal background as PNH, another immune-mediated marrow failure state. In contrast, mutations in DNMT3A, ASXL1, TP53, RUNX1, and CSMD1 are unfavorable, these patients have a lower response rate to immunosuppressive therapy and a survival curve that separates sharply from the unmutated and favorable groups, with an overall survival difference around p equals 0.008 over long-term follow up. The mosaic plot shows that patients with unfavorable mutations have a much higher rate of no response and lower complete response compared to those with favorable mutations or no mutations. Clinically, this reinforces why some clonal evolution in aplastic anemia is not necessarily ominous, a PIGA or BCOR clone can actually reflect an immune escape mechanism rather than pre-leukemic transformation, whereas DNMT3A or TP53 clones raise concern for evolution toward secondary MDS or AML.

keypoints: ~30% of AA patients have MDS-related somatic mutations
Favorable: PIGA, BCOR, BCORL1 → better IST response, better OS
Unfavorable: DNMT3A, ASXL1, TP53, RUNX1, CSMD1 → worse OS (p=0.008)
BCOR/BCORL1 clones share biology with PNH immune escape
segments.voiceover: Roughly a third of aplastic anemia patients harbor MDS-related somatic mutations. The ones to memorize as favorable are PIGA, BCOR, and BCORL1, which predict a better response to immunosuppressive therapy and better overall survival. The unfavorable group is DNMT3A, ASXL1, TP53, RUNX1, and CSMD1, which predicts a lower response rate and significantly worse survival. Think of BCOR and PIGA clones as an immune escape phenomenon rather than pre-leukemic change.

This slide maps out how somatic mutations distribute across PNH, aplastic anemia, and MDS, and it's really testing whether you understand the overlap syndrome. Comparing aplastic anemia to MDS, aplastic anemia patients frequently carry BCOR or BCORL1 mutations, which are relatively specific to the immune-mediated marrow failure setting, and PNH clones driven by PIGA mutations are found in twenty to thirty percent of aplastic anemia patients and post-aplastic anemia MDS, but are rare, only about two percent, in primary hypocellular MDS. That distinction is a great board discriminator: a sizable PNH clone points you toward aplastic anemia or PNH itself rather than primary MDS. When you compare secondary MDS arising after aplastic anemia to primary hypocellular MDS, RUNX1, SETBP1, ASXL1, and deletion seven or seven q are more prevalent in post-aplastic anemia secondary MDS, while classic spliceosomal mutations, SF3B1, SRSF2, ZRSR2, and U2AF1, are relatively absent in secondary MDS compared to primary MDS. So the overall teaching point is that clonal evolution after immunosuppressive therapy for aplastic anemia follows a different mutational route than de novo MDS, favoring BCOR, RUNX1, and monosomy seven rather than the spliceosomal pathway.

keypoints: PNH clones: 20-30% in AA/post-AA-MDS vs only ~2% in primary hypo-MDS
BCOR/BCORL1 mutations frequent in AA, less so in de novo MDS
Post-AA secondary MDS: ↑RUNX1, SETBP1, ASXL1, del(7)/7q
Secondary MDS relatively lacks spliceosomal mutations (SF3B1, SRSF2, ZRSR2, U2AF1)
segments.voiceover: A large PNH clone, twenty to thirty percent, favors aplastic anemia or post-aplastic anemia MDS, while primary hypocellular MDS rarely shows a PNH clone. BCOR and BCORL1 mutations are enriched in aplastic anemia. When aplastic anemia evolves into secondary MDS, expect RUNX1, SETBP1, ASXL1, and deletion seven or seven q, but notably an absence of the spliceosomal mutations typical of primary MDS, like SF3B1 and SRSF2.

This is the etiologic classification of aplastic anemia, and it's worth organizing into acquired versus hereditary causes. Most acquired aplastic anemia is idiopathic and thought to be autoimmune, a T-cell mediated attack on hematopoietic stem cells, which is why immunosuppressive therapy works. Drug causes to remember include NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, certain antibiotics like chloramphenicol, antithyroid drugs, and gold compounds. Toxins include benzene, chlorinated hydrocarbons, and organophosphates. Viral triggers include EBV, parvovirus B19, and seronegative hepatitis, meaning hepatitis that's non-A through non-G, as well as HIV. Other acquired associations include paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria itself, autoimmune and connective tissue disorders such as eosinophilic fasciitis, Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus, as well as thymoma, pregnancy, and iatrogenic causes like radiation and cytotoxic chemotherapy. Critically, the diagnosis of aplastic anemia requires you to exclude hypocellular MDS, PNH, large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and lymphoma, since these can all mimic a hypocellular marrow. The hereditary causes, which you must screen for especially in younger patients, are Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.

keypoints: Most acquired AA is idiopathic/autoimmune (T-cell mediated)
Drug triggers: NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, antithyroids, gold, chloramphenicol
Must exclude hypocellular MDS, PNH, LGLL, lymphoma before diagnosing AA
Hereditary causes: Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond, CAMT
segments.voiceover: Most acquired aplastic anemia is idiopathic and autoimmune. Remember the drug list, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, antithyroid drugs, gold, and chloramphenicol, plus viral triggers like parvovirus B19 and seronegative hepatitis. Before you diagnose aplastic anemia, you must rule out hypocellular MDS, PNH, large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and lymphoma. And always screen younger patients for hereditary causes, Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.

This summary table of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes is extremely high yield and often tested by matching clinical triad to gene to diagnostic test. Fanconi anemia presents with skin pigmentation changes, short stature, radial ray and thumb abnormalities, and craniofacial, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, or cardiac anomalies, plus aplastic anemia and a strong predisposition to AML and solid tumors like squamous cell carcinoma, brain tumors, and Wilms tumor. It's inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern through genes like FANCA, FANCC, and several others, with one X-linked gene, FANCB, and the diagnostic test is chromosome breakage studies using agents like diepoxybutane. Dyskeratosis congenita has the classic triad of abnormal nails, reticular skin pigmentation, and oral leukoplakia, with predisposition to marrow failure, malignancy, and pulmonary fibrosis. It can be X-linked recessive through DKC1, autosomal dominant through TERC, TERT, or TINF2, or autosomal recessive, and the diagnostic test is telomere length measurement, since these are telomerase complex defects. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome combines exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with bone marrow failure and skeletal anomalies, is autosomal recessive through SBDS, and is diagnosed with serum trypsinogen and pancreatic isoamylase levels. Finally, congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia presents in the neonatal period with bleeding and carries AML risk, is autosomal recessive through c-MPL, the thrombopoietin receptor gene, and shows a normal cellular marrow but absent megakaryocytes.

keypoints: Fanconi anemia: chromosome breakage test, AR (FANCA/C/etc), ↑AML/solid tumor risk
Dyskeratosis congenita: triad of nails/rash/leukoplakia, telomere length test
Shwachman-Diamond: exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, ↓trypsinogen/isoamylase, SBDS gene
CAMT: neonatal bleeding, absent megakaryocytes, c-MPL mutation
segments.voiceover: Match each syndrome to its test. Fanconi anemia is diagnosed with chromosome breakage studies and features radial ray anomalies plus high AML and solid tumor risk. Dyskeratosis congenita has the nails, reticular rash, and leukoplakia triad, diagnosed by telomere length. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome combines exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with marrow failure, confirmed by serum trypsinogen and pancreatic isoamylase. And congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia presents with neonatal bleeding, absent megakaryocytes on a normal cellular marrow, and a c-MPL mutation.

This is the algorithm for severe aplastic anemia, and it is heavily tested. First exclude other causes, discontinue any offending drug, and give supportive care with transfusion, antibiotics, and G-CSF. The real branch point is whether the patient has an HLA-matched sibling. If yes and age is under about forty, go straight to sibling bone marrow transplant, with five-year overall survival eighty-two percent under twenty, seventy-two percent for twenty to forty, and dropping to fifty-one percent over forty. If no matched sibling, or an older patient, first-line is immunosuppressive therapy — horse ATG plus cyclosporine — because horse ATG clearly outperforms rabbit ATG, with response rate sixty-eight versus thirty-seven percent and overall survival ninety-six versus seventy-six percent. Adding eltrombopag to standard ATG plus cyclosporine, per the RACE trial, boosts six-month overall response to sixty-eight percent, complete response to forty-one percent, and two-year overall survival to ninety percent. Younger patients under twenty with no sibling donor who fail IST move to unrelated donor transplant, which has excellent five-year survival under forty at over sixty-six percent, but declines with age. If IST fails at day plus one-twenty in an older or no-donor patient, options include alternate donor transplant or a second course of ATG plus cyclosporine, anabolic steroids, eltrombopag, and supportive care. Remember the two hATG formulations: lymphoglobulin at fifteen milligrams per kilogram per day for five days, and ATGAM at forty milligrams per kilogram per day for four days.

keypoints: HLA-matched sib + age <40 → sibling BMT first-line
No sib donor → horse ATG+CsA (RR 60-70%, 5y-OS ~75%)
Horse ATG beats rabbit ATG: RR 68% vs 37%, OS 96% vs 76%
+Eltrombopag (RACE): 6m-ORR 68%, CRR 41%, 2y-OS 90%
Fail IST at d+120 → alt donor Tx or 2nd ATG+CsA
segments.voiceover: Key points for severe aplastic anemia management. A matched sibling donor under age forty goes straight to sibling transplant. Without a sibling donor, first-line is horse ATG plus cyclosporine, since horse ATG beats rabbit ATG with response rate sixty-eight versus thirty-seven percent and survival ninety-six versus seventy-six percent. Adding eltrombopag per the RACE trial raises six-month overall response to sixty-eight percent, complete response to forty-one percent, and two-year survival to ninety percent. If immunosuppression fails at day plus one-twenty, move to alternate donor transplant or a second round of ATG and cyclosporine.

Pure red cell aplasia is a normochromic, macrocytic anemia with severe reticulocytopenia under one percent, and bone marrow showing erythroblasts absent or under one percent — everything else in the marrow is normal. About forty percent of cases have a circulating erythropoiesis inhibitor in the plasma. For boards, memorize the classification. Congenital causes include Diamond-Blackfan anemia, inherited, with RPS19 or DBA1 mutations found in about twenty-five percent, versus the non-inherited Pearson syndrome. Acquired primary PRCA is usually autoimmune, including transient erythroblastopenia of childhood. The classic secondary association is thymoma, which is T-cell mediated — always screen a new PRCA patient for thymoma with chest imaging. Also link PRCA to hematologic malignancies like CLL, and to infections — the single most important is human parvovirus B19, which directly infects erythroid progenitors via the P antigen receptor; the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts with nuclear inclusions. B19-associated PRCA classically causes transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolysis, and is treated with IVIG. Other notable secondary causes include post-transplant anti-ABO antibodies and anti-erythropoietin antibodies after EPO therapy. Treatment: stop offending drugs, control infection with IVIG for parvovirus, replace B12 and folate, thymectomy for thymoma-associated cases with about forty percent response, and immunosuppression — prednisone, cyclosporine which has the best response rate at sixty-five to eighty percent, cyclophosphamide or azathioprine, ATG, IVIG, or splenectomy as later options.

keypoints: PRCA = macrocytic anemia, retic <1%, marrow erythroblasts <1%
Diamond-Blackfan: RPS19/DBA1 mutation in 25%
Thymoma (T-cell mediated) — always screen with imaging
Parvovirus B19 → giant pronormoblasts; Tx = IVIG
Immunosuppression: cyclosporine best RR 65-80%
segments.voiceover: Key points on pure red cell aplasia. It is a macrocytic anemia with reticulocytes under one percent and marrow erythroblasts absent or under one percent. Diamond-Blackfan anemia has RPS19 or DBA1 mutations in about a quarter of cases. Thymoma is the classic secondary association and is T-cell mediated, so always screen with chest imaging. Parvovirus B19 causes giant pronormoblasts with nuclear inclusions and is treated with IVIG. For immunosuppression, cyclosporine has the best response rate, around sixty-five to eighty percent.

This algorithm separates erythrocytosis, an increased erythrocyte concentration that includes relative causes like hemoconcentration or Gaisbock syndrome, from true polycythemia, an increased red cell mass. Work-up starts with serum EPO and JAK2 V617F. If EPO is high, that argues against polycythemia vera and points toward secondary causes: aberrant EPO production from hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, uterine cancer, adrenal adenoma, or Cushing syndrome; or chronic hypoxia from COPD, sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, cyanotic congenital heart disease, hypoventilation, high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobinopathy, or high altitude. If EPO is normal or low, test JAK2 V617F — if positive, that essentially confirms polycythemia vera, since JAK2 V617F is found in over ninety-five percent of PV. If negative, reflexively test for JAK2 exon 12 mutations, which are found in most of the remaining JAK2-negative PV cases with an isolated erythrocytosis phenotype. If exon 12 is also negative, proceed to bone marrow biopsy; findings there combined with the EPO level differentiate familial PV or PFCP with low EPO, familial erythrocytosis with normal EPO if the biopsy is unremarkable, or MPN-unclassifiable if the biopsy shows myeloproliferative changes with normal EPO. This algorithm is a favorite board question because it forces you to sequence JAK2 testing correctly — V617F first, then exon 12 if negative — before invoking bone marrow biopsy.

keypoints: Erythrocytosis = ↑RBC concentration; Polycythemia = ↑RBC mass
JAK2 V617F(+) in >95% of PV — test first
JAK2(-) with high suspicion → test exon 12 mutations next
High EPO → screen for tumor (RCC, HCC) or chronic hypoxia
BM biopsy reserved for JAK2(-) cases to sort PV-mimics
segments.voiceover: Key points on the polycythemia work-up. Erythrocytosis means increased red cell concentration, while true polycythemia means increased red cell mass. JAK2 V617F is positive in over ninety-five percent of polycythemia vera, so test it first. If negative, move to JAK2 exon 12 mutations before considering bone marrow biopsy. A high serum EPO should prompt a search for a tumor producing EPO or a chronic hypoxic condition. Bone marrow biopsy is reserved for JAK2-negative cases to distinguish familial PV, familial erythrocytosis, and MPN-unclassifiable.

This table is classic image-recognition material for boards — you need to match RBC shape to disease at a glance. Spherocytes are spheric with no central pallor and look microcytic; think hereditary spherocytosis or immune hemolytic anemia. Elliptocytes are oval, seen in hereditary elliptocytosis and megaloblastic anemia. Stomatocytes have a slit-like rather than round central pallor, classically from alcoholism or chronic liver disease, and also hereditary stomatocytosis. Acanthocytes, or spur cells, have five to ten irregular spicules of variable length and spacing — associate these with liver disease and abetalipoproteinemia. Echinocytes, or burr cells, have ten to thirty small, evenly spaced spicules, seen in uremia, pyruvate kinase deficiency, or as an artifact. Sickle cells are diagnostic of HbSS or HbSC disease. Target cells have a bullseye of central density and appear in thalassemia, hemoglobin C disorders, iron deficiency, liver disease, post-splenectomy, and LCAT deficiency. Schistocytes are the fragmented, helmet-shaped small cells of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, turbulent flow states like mechanical valves, and hemolytic uremic syndrome — always check a smear for schistocytes when you suspect TTP or HUS or DIC. The key exam trap is distinguishing spur cells, irregular and fewer, from burr cells, regular and numerous — spur cells mean liver disease, burr cells mean uremia or artifact.

keypoints: Spherocyte: no central pallor → HS, AIHA
Acanthocyte/spur cell (irregular spicules) → liver dz, abetalipoproteinemia
Echinocyte/burr cell (regular spicules) → uremia, PK deficiency, artifact
Target cell → thalassemia, liver dz, post-splenectomy
Schistocyte → MAHA, TTP/HUS, mechanical valve
segments.voiceover: Key points for RBC morphology. Spherocytes lack central pallor and point to hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The classic exam trap is spur cells versus burr cells — spur cells have irregular, variable spicules and mean liver disease or abetalipoproteinemia, while burr cells have regular, numerous spicules and mean uremia, pyruvate kinase deficiency, or artifact. Target cells suggest thalassemia, liver disease, or post-splenectomy state. Schistocytes are the hallmark of microangiopathic hemolysis, so think TTP, HUS, DIC, or a mechanical valve.

This slide covers RBC inclusion bodies — high-yield because boards love asking what an inclusion is made of and what stain reveals it. Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants, a single round basophilic dot, classically seen after splenectomy or with hyposplenism, as well as megaloblastic anemia and hemolysis — the spleen normally pits these out, so their presence signals impaired splenic function. Basophilic stippling is residual RNA and ribosomes, seen in lead intoxication, thalassemia, and other abnormal heme synthesis states like sickle cell disease or MDS. Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing siderotic granules, visible on Prussian blue stain, seen after splenectomy, in hemolysis, sideroblastic anemia, and MDS. HbH bodies are beta-globin tetramers, beta-4, visible only with supravital stain, giving a golf-ball appearance, and are diagnostic of HbH disease in alpha thalassemia. Heinz bodies are precipitated denatured hemoglobin, supravital stain only, classically from G6PD deficiency under oxidant stress, unstable hemoglobin in alpha thalassemia, and chronic liver disease. Fessas bodies are alpha-globin tetramers, alpha-4, supravital only, specific for beta-thalassemia major. Crystals indicate hemoglobin C disease. Cabot rings are mitotic spindle remnants, seen in MDS and megaloblastic anemia. The key distinction to memorize: DNA is Howell-Jolly, RNA is basophilic stippling, and iron is Pappenheimer — same post-splenectomy setting but three different stains and contents.

keypoints: Howell-Jolly body = DNA → post-splenectomy/hyposplenism
Basophilic stippling = RNA → lead poisoning, thalassemia
Pappenheimer body = Iron (Prussian blue) → splenectomy, sideroblastic anemia
HbH body (β4) vs Fessas body (α4) — supravital stain only
Heinz body = denatured Hb → G6PD deficiency, oxidant stress
segments.voiceover: Key points on RBC inclusion bodies. Howell-Jolly bodies are DNA remnants seen after splenectomy or hyposplenism. Basophilic stippling is RNA, classic for lead poisoning and thalassemia. Pappenheimer bodies are iron granules on Prussian blue stain, also linked to splenectomy and sideroblastic anemia. HbH bodies are beta-four tetramers marking HbH disease, while Fessas bodies are alpha-four tetramers marking beta-thalassemia major, both visible only with supravital stain. Heinz bodies are denatured hemoglobin, the hallmark of G6PD deficiency under oxidant stress.
